claim: The size of the nucleus scales robustly with cell size so that the nuclear-to-cell volume ratio (N/C ratio) is maintained during cell growth in many cell types.
source: The size of the nucleus scales robustly with cell size so that the nuclear-to-cell volume ratio (N/C ratio) is maintained during cell growth in many cell types.
evidence: This is a general statement about nuclear scaling supported by the literature and the study's own findings.

claim: The N/C ratio is not determined by DNA amount but is instead influenced by factors such as nuclear envelope mechanics and nuclear transport.
source: Previous studies have established that the N/C ratio is not determined by DNA amount but is instead influenced by factors such as nuclear envelope mechanics and nuclear transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: The N/C ratio is determined by the numbers of macromolecules in the nucleoplasm and cytoplasm.
source: This model posits that the N/C ratio is determined by the numbers of macromolecules in the nucleoplasm and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is the central theoretical claim of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fission yeast nucleus behaves as an ideal osmometer whose volume is primarily dictated by osmotic forces.
source: Osmotic shift experiments showed that the fission yeast nucleus behaves as an ideal osmometer whose volume is primarily dictated by osmotic forces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from osmotic shift experiments.

claim: Inhibition of nuclear export caused accumulation of macromolecules in the nucleoplasm, leading to nuclear swelling.
source: Inhibition of nuclear export caused accumulation of macromolecules in the nucleoplasm, leading to nuclear swelling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LMB treatment experiments.

claim: The N/C ratio is maintained by a homeostasis mechanism based upon synthesis of macromolecules during growth.
source: We further demonstrated that the N/C ratio is maintained by a homeostasis mechanism based upon synthesis of macromolecules during growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and modeling of N/C ratio homeostasis.

claim: Nuclear size scaling has been documented across the eukaryotic domain since initial observations in plants.
source: Since the initial observation in plants (Strasburger, 1893) the scaling of nuclear and cell volume has been documented across the eukaryotic domain (Conklin, 1912; Gregory, 2005; Moore et al., 2019; Neumann and Nurse, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to historical and recent literature.

claim: Scaling of nuclear size was observed for nucleoids in prokaryotes.
source: More recently, scaling was even observed for nucleoids in prokaryotes (Gray et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: In multicellular organisms, the nuclear-to-cell volume (N/C) ratio varies among cell types, but this ratio is generally maintained as a constant within a given cell type.
source: In multicellular organisms, the nuclear-to-cell volume (N/C) ratio varies among cell types, but this ratio is generally maintained as a constant within a given cell type (Conklin, 1912; Hertwig, 1903).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: During cell growth, the N/C ratio is maintained through much of the cell cycle as the nucleus grows in volume at the same rate as the cell.
source: During cell growth, the N/C ratio is also maintained through much of the cell cycle (Jorgensen et al., 2007; Neumann and Nurse, 2007; Willis et al., 2016), as the nucleus grows in volume at the same rate as the cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Abnormal N/C ratios are a hallmark of diseases such as certain cancers and are sometimes used as diagnostic criteria.
source: Abnormal N/C ratios are a hallmark of diseases such as certain cancers and are sometimes used as diagnostic criteria (Foraker, 1954; Slater et al., 2005; Webster et al., 2009; Zink et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to medical literature.

claim: The N/C ratio may play an important role in regulatory mechanisms, for instance, in the mid-blastula transition in embryonic development.
source: The N/C ratio may play an important role in regulatory mechanisms, for instance, in the mid-blastula transition in embryonic development (Amodeo et al., 2015; Jevtić and Levy, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents a speculative connection.

claim: DNA is unlikely to be the rate-limiting structural component that determines nuclear size.
source: Thus, DNA is unlikely to be the rate-limiting structural component that determines nuclear size.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from multiple lines of evidence presented in the preceding text.

claim: DNA is only a minor component in the nucleus by volume, estimated to occupy <1% of the nuclear volume.
source: DNA is only a minor component in the nucleus by volume; it has been estimated to occupy <1% of the nuclear volume and is many times less abundant in the nucleus than RNA (Milo and Phillips, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a reference source.

claim: Nuclear size does increase with increased ploidy in a given cell type, but generally this increase is accompanied by a similar increase in cell size.
source: Nuclear size does increase with increased ploidy in a given cell type, but generally this increase is accompanied by a similar increase in cell size (Cavalier-Smith, 2005; Gregory, 2005; Gregory and Mable, 2005; Jorgensen et al., 2007; Robinson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: During the cell cycle, nuclear size continues to grow in the G2 phase even when DNA content is no longer increasing.
source: During the cell cycle, nuclear size continues to grow in the G2 phase even when DNA content is no longer increasing (Jorgensen et al., 2007; Neumann and Nurse, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells with DNA content ranging from 2N to 32N have a similar N/C ratio in fission yeast.
source: Further, through manipulating genome content in fission yeast, it has been shown that cells with DNA content ranging from 2N to 32N have a similar N/C ratio (Neumann and Nurse, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Nuclear volume and surface area can be uncoupled and are regulated independently.
source: It is clear however that nuclear volume and surface area can be uncoupled and are regulated independently.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from examples provided in the text.

claim: Arrest of budding yeast cells in mitosis can lead to continued growth of the nuclear envelope without growth in nuclear volume, leading to misshapen nuclei and formation of nuclear envelope protrusions.
source: For instance, arrest of budding yeast cells in mitosis can lead to continued growth of the nuclear envelope without growth in nuclear volume, leading to misshapen nuclei and formation of nuclear envelope protrusions (Webster et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Growth of the nuclear envelope may occur through the transfer of membranes from the endoplasmic reticulum or by lipid assembly at the nuclear envelope.
source: Growth of the nuclear envelope may occur through the transfer of membranes from the endoplasmic reticulum or by lipid assembly at the nuclear envelope (Blank et al., 2017; Hirano et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents possible mechanisms.

claim: Nuclear volume, not surface area, is the relevant geometric parameter that is maintained for the N/C ratio.
source: Studies have shown, however, that nuclear volume, not surface area, is the relevant geometric parameter that is maintained for the N/C ratio (Cantwell and Nurse, 2019a; Neumann and Nurse, 2007; Walters et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Genome-wide screens in fission yeast have demonstrated that mutants in the vast majority of genes exhibit normal N/C ratios.
source: Genome-wide screens in fission yeast have demonstrated that mutants in the vast majority of genes exhibit normal N/C ratios, ruling out many possible cellular processes and molecular pathways (Cantwell and Nurse, 2019b; Kume et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genome-wide screen studies.

claim: The N/C ratio is independent of cell size, shape, and number of nuclei.
source: For instance, the N/C ratio is independent of cell size, shape, and number of nuclei (Neumann and Nurse, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Screens have identified only a small number of genes that impact the N/C ratio, mostly related to nuclear transport or lipid synthesis.
source: Screens have so far identified only a small number of genes that impact the N/C ratio, mostly related to nuclear transport or lipid synthesis (Cantwell and Nurse, 2019b; Kume et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to screen studies.

claim: Lamins and chromatin factors have been implicated in the control of nuclear size and shape in vertebrate cell systems.
source: In vertebrate cell systems, lamins and chromatin factors have been implicated in the control of nuclear size and shape (Edens et al., 2017; Levy and Heald, 2010; Muchir et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in vertebrate systems.

claim: Depletion of lamin in Xenopus eggs extract resulted in a reduction of nuclear size and formation of abnormal nuclear shapes.
source: For example, depletion of lamin in Xenopus eggs extract resulted in a reduction of nuclear size and formation of abnormal nuclear shapes (Newport et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Yeast lack lamins, making it unlikely that nuclear lamins represent a universal mechanism for nuclear size control.
source: However, as yeast lack lamins, it is unlikely that the nuclear lamins themselves represent a universal mechanism for nuclear size control.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about yeast biology and inference about universal mechanisms.

claim: The rounded shape of the typical nucleus suggests there may be slightly higher osmotic pressure in the nucleoplasm compared to the cytoplasm, which is balanced by the nuclear membrane tension.
source: The rounded shape of the typical nucleus suggests there may be slightly higher osmotic pressure in the nucleoplasm compared to the cytoplasm, which is balanced by the nuclear membrane tension.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed shape of nuclei.

claim: Colloid osmotic pressures are produced by the distinct sets of macromolecules in the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: These pressures likely arise from macromolecular crowding forces termed 'colloid osmotic pressure', which are produced by the distinct sets of macromolecules in the nucleus and cytoplasm (Mitchison, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a theoretical framework.

claim: Treatment of cells with osmotic shocks causes both the cell and nucleus to swell and shrink.
source: Treatment of cells with osmotic shocks causes both the cell and nucleus to swell and shrink (Churney, 1942).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a classic experiment.

claim: Injection of crowding agents such as polyethylene glycol into the cytoplasm cause shrinkage of the nucleus.
source: Classic experiments demonstrated that injection of crowding agents such as polyethylene glycol into the cytoplasm cause shrinkage of the nucleus (Harding and Feldherr, 1958; Harding and Feldherr, 1959).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classic experiments.

claim: Isolated nuclei are responsive to osmotic shifts but the osmotic behavior depends on the molecular size of the osmolytes such that only macromolecules larger than 30 kDa will affect their volumes.
source: Isolated nuclei are also responsive to osmotic shifts but the osmotic behavior depends on the molecular size of the osmolytes such that only macromolecules larger than 30 kDa will affect their volumes (Finan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The cell is inflated by turgor pressure, which is defined as the osmotic pressure difference across the plasma membrane balanced by the elastic wall surrounding the cell.
source: The cell is inflated by turgor pressure, which is defined as the osmotic pressure difference across the plasma membrane (Cout, CCy) balanced by the elastic wall surrounding the cell.
evidence: This is a definition based on established biophysical principles.

claim: Turgor pressure is produced largely from small molecules, such as ions and metabolites, attracting water into the cell through osmosis.
source: Turgor pressure is produced largely from small molecules, such as ions and metabolites, attracting water into the cell through osmosis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of osmotic principles.

claim: The nuclear envelope is a semi-permeable membrane with pores that allow water, ions and other small molecules to pass with a Stoke radius below <2.5 nm.
source: The nuclear envelope is a semi-permeable membrane with pores that allow water, ions and other small molecules to pass with a Stoke radius below <2.5 nm (Mohr et al., 2009), but remains relatively impermeable to large proteins, macromolecular complexes, DNA and RNA, with the exception of specific nuclear transport mechanisms through nuclear pores.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about nuclear pore properties.

claim: Macromolecules produce colloid osmotic pressures by attracting a shell of water around them.
source: Macromolecules produce colloid osmotic pressures, by attracting a shell of water around them (Mitchison, 2019; Vink, 1971; Vink, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Colloid osmotic pressures are estimated to be orders of magnitude smaller than turgor pressure (kPa versus MPa in yeast).
source: These pressures are estimated to be orders of magnitude smaller than turgor pressure (kPa versus MPa in yeast).
evidence: This is an estimate based on theoretical considerations.

claim: The N/C ratio is relatively insensitive to osmotic shocks for small values of nuclear membrane tension independently of cell membrane tension.
source: The results also reveal that the N/C ratio is relatively insensitive to osmotic shocks for small values of σN independently of σC (σN = 0.5 mN/m, Figure 1C and D, Appendix 1 and 3).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: In the limiting case of negligible nuclear membrane tension and balanced normalized non-osmotic volumes, the N/C ratio is set simply by the ratio of the apparent numbers of osmotically active molecules in the nucleoplasm and in the whole cell.
source: As explained in Appendix 4, in this case the N/C ratio is set simply by the ratio of the apparent numbers of osmotically active molecules in the nucleoplasm and in the whole cell
evidence: This is a mathematical result derived in the appendix.

claim: Hyperosmotic shifts of various sorbitol concentrations caused sizable decrease (up to ~54%) in volume of fission yeast cells.
source: Hyperosmotic shifts of various sorbitol concentrations caused sizable decrease (up to ~54%) in volume of cells, as previously noted (Atilgan et al., 2015; Knapp et al., 2019; Molines et al., 2022, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data and citations.

claim: The volume responses of whole fission yeast cells to osmotic shifts were non-linear, indicative of a non-ideal osmometer behavior.
source: The BVH plot showed that the volume responses were non-linear, indicative of a non-ideal osmometer behavior (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from BVH plot analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The non-linear volume responses of whole cells were consistent with the actions of the elastic cell wall that exerts compressive forces on the cell body and resists large expansions of volume.
source: The relationships were non-linear for both hyper- and hypotonic responses, consistent with the actions of the elastic cell wall that exerts compressive forces on the cell body and resists large expansions of volume (Atilgan et al., 2015; Davì and Minc, 2015; Schaber and Klipp, 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data supported by citations.

claim: Protoplasts in isotonic conditions (YE +0.4 M sorbitol) exhibited similar average volumes as those of walled cells in YE +0 M sorbitol.
source: At this concentration of sorbitol, an asynchronous population of protoplasts exhibited similar average volumes as those of walled cells in YE +0 M sorbitol, and similar cytoplasmic concentrations as assessed by fluorescence intensity of a cytoplasmic marker E2-mCrimson (Methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B, Al-Sady et al., 2016; Knapp et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: Protoplasts were able to swell up to 40% in volume or shrink 40% without bursting.
source: These methods allowed for quantitative probing of osmotic effects over a remarkable ~3 fold range of volume; notably, protoplasts were able to swell up to 40% in volume or shrink 40% without bursting.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about protoplast behavior.

claim: The BVH plot of protoplast responses showed a linear behavior through a range of sorbitol concentrations, indicative of an ideal osmometer.
source: The BVH plot of protoplast responses showed a linear behavior through this range of sorbitol concentrations (Figure 2D), indicative of an ideal osmometer.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from BVH plot analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The osmotic shift experiments allowed estimation of S. pombe solute concentration at ~30 × 10^7 solutes/µm^3, which represents an osmolarity of 500±45 mOsmol.
source: As the number of osmolytes is directly related to cell volume in osmotic shift experiments for ideal osmometers, this allowed us to estimate S. pombe solute concentration at ~30 × 107 solutes/µm3, which represents an osmolarity of 500±45 mOsmol (Methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–G).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement derived from experimental data.

claim: In hyperosmotic shifts, nuclei in both whole cells and protoplasts shrank into an abnormal involuted shape, suggesting a loss in volume but not surface area.
source: In hyperosmotic shifts, nuclei in both whole cells and protoplasts shrank into an abnormal involuted shape, suggesting a loss in volume but not surface area (Figure 2A and B), similar to what has been observed in mammalian cells (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by images and citation.

claim: In hypoosmotic shifts with protoplasts, nuclei were able to expand in <1 min into a spherical shape with an increase up to 40% in volume and 26% in surface area.
source: Strinkingly, in hypoosmotic shifts with protoplasts, nuclei were able to expand in <1 min into a spherical shape with an increase up to 40% in volume and 26% in surface area (Figure 2B and E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 2B and E.

claim: The large rapid expansion of the nuclear envelope suggested that the nuclear envelope can draw upon membrane stores, potentially from the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: This large rapid expansion of the nuclear envelope suggested that the nuclear envelope can draw upon membrane stores, potentially from the endoplasmic reticulum (Fricker et al., 1997; Kume et al., 2019; Roubinet et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from experimental observations, supported by citations.

claim: BVH plots showed that the volume of nuclei in protoplasts followed a linear behavior in osmotic shifts over a 3-fold range of volumes.
source: BVH plots showed that the volume of nuclei in protoplasts followed a linear behavior in osmotic shifts over an impressive 3-fold range of volumes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from BVH plot analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The linear response of nuclear volume to osmotic shifts showed that the nucleus behaved as an ideal osmometer.
source: Importantly, this linear response showed that the nucleus behaved as an ideal osmometer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the linear BVH plot data.

claim: The ideal osmometer behavior of the nucleus implied that tension of the nuclear envelope was negligible on nuclear size (σN ≈ 0 N/m).
source: This finding implied that tension of the nuclear envelope was negligible on nuclear size: σN ≈ 0 N/m; the nuclear envelope does not exert tension that alters the volume response to osmotic forces, so that nuclear volume is directly responsive to its osmotic environment.
evidence: This is an inference from the ideal osmometer behavior observed experimentally.

claim: The protoplast and the nucleus approximate two nested spherical ideal osmometers as described in the theoretical model.
source: Thus, these experimental findings show that the protoplast and the nucleus approximate two nested spherical ideal osmometers as described in our theoretical model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The nucleus in whole cells (those with intact cell walls) are also ideal osmometers.
source: As the physical properties of the nucleus are unlikely to change in the short amount of time needed to remove the cell wall, these results imply that the nucleus in whole cells (those with intact cell walls) are also ideal osmometers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the protoplast experiments.

claim: There was no significant change in the N/C ratio before and after cell wall removal.
source: There was no significant change in the N/C ratio before and after cell wall removal (Figure 3A, left panel).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: The N/C ratio is independent of the outer tension of the system (σC).
source: Thus, as predicted by our model, the N/C ratio is independent of the outer tension of the system (σC).
evidence: This is a conclusion from experimental data that confirms a model prediction.

claim: The N/C ratio does not change with the osmotic concentration of the media.
source: These results demonstrated that the N/C ratio does not change with the osmotic concentration of the media, confirming the predictions of the model that the sizes of the cell and nucleus are both regulated by osmotic pressures.
evidence: This is a conclusion from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cytoplasmic GEMs displayed subdiffusive motion with an anomalous diffusive exponent α~0.9 comparable to measurements in HEK293, hPNE cells and S. cerevisiae.
source: Mean square displacement (MSD) curves showed that the cytoplasmic GEMs displayed subdiffusive motion with an anomalous diffusive exponent α~0.9 comparable to measurements in HEK293, hPNE cells and S. cerevisiae (Delarue et al., 2018; Szoradi et al., 2021, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by MSD analysis and citations.

claim: Nucleoplasmic GEMs exhibited a stronger subdiffusive behavior with α~0.8, suggesting a stronger caging effect compared to the cytoplasm.
source: Nucleoplasmic GEMs exhibited a stronger subdiffusive behavior with α~0.8, suggesting a stronger caging effect compared to the cytoplasm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with interpretation.

claim: Nuclear GEMs consistently exhibited significantly higher effective diffusion coefficient than cytoplasmic GEMs (DNeff ~0.55 µm2/s and DCyeff ~0.40 µm2/s).
source: Notably, nuclear GEMs consistently exhibited significantly higher Deff than cytoplasmic GEMs (DNeff ~0.55 µm2/s and DCyeff ~0.40 µm2/s, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At the 40 nm size scale, the ability of particles to diffuse is somewhat different in the nucleoplasm versus cytoplasm.
source: These results demonstrated that at the 40 nm size scale, the ability of particles to diffuse is somewhat different in the nucleoplasm versus cytoplasm; these differences may reflect the differences in composition and nanoscale organization between nucleoplasm and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion from GEMs diffusion measurements with interpretation.

claim: Protoplasts in isotonic conditions exhibited similar effective diffusion coefficient and anomalous exponent in the cytoplasm as whole cells, showing that cytoplasmic properties probed by GEMs were not affected by removal of the cell wall.
source: We also assessed cytoplasmic states in protoplasts compared to those in whole cells. Protoplasts in isotonic conditions exhibited similar Deff and α in the cytoplasm, showing that cytoplasmic properties probed by GEMs were not affected by removal of the cell wall (Figure 4D, black arrow; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation comparing protoplasts and whole cells.

claim: Effective diffusion coefficient of the cytoplasmic GEMs in protoplasts exhibited an exponential relationship with medium concentration and hence macromolecular concentration.
source: We found that Deff of the cytoplasmic GEMs in protoplasts exhibited an exponential relationship with medium concentration and hence macromolecular concentration (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The relationship between effective diffusion coefficient and concentration could be fit with a Phillies' model.
source: This relationship could be fit with a Phillies' model (Masaro and Zhu, 1999; Phillies, 1988) which uses a unique stretched exponential equation to describe a tracer particle's self-diffusive behavior in a wide range of polymer concentrations (Methods, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a modeling result fitting experimental data, supported by citations.

claim: The normalized effective diffusion coefficient and anomalous exponent values of cytoGEMS and nucGEMs were similar in cells treated with varying doses of sorbitol.
source: Indeed, even though the absolute values between cytoGEMs and nucGEMs Deff were slightly different, the normalized Deff and α values of cytoGEMS and nucGEMs were similar in cells treated with varying doses of sorbitol (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4E and supplementary figures.

claim: GEMs can be used to inform on relative changes in the concentration of macromolecules and resultant colloid osmotic pressures within each compartment.
source: Together, these findings showed that GEMs can be used to inform on relative changes in the concentration of macromolecules and resultant colloid osmotic pressures within each compartment; for example, both environments showed consistent behavior without evidence for sharp transitions in biophysical properties such as phase transitions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the GEMs experiments.

claim: Inhibition of nuclear export leads to an increase in nuclear size, either through treatment with leptomycin B or through mutants affecting the nuclear transport machinery.
source: It has been previously reported that inhibition of nuclear export leads to an increase in nuclear size, either through treatment with a drug leptomycin B (LMB, an inhibitor of the Crm1 exportin) or through mutants affecting the nuclear transport machinery (Kudo et al., 1999; Kume et al., 2017; Neumann and Nurse, 2007; Yoshida and Horinouchi, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LMB causes the redistribution of only a small subset of proteins in Xenopus oocytes.
source: LMB causes the redistribution of only a small subset of proteins in Xenopus oocytes (Wühr et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Upon LMB treatment, interphase fission yeast cells continued to grow at a similar rate as untreated cells, but their nucleus grew even faster.
source: Upon LMB treatment, interphase fission yeast cells continued to grow at a similar rate as untreated cells, but their nucleus grew even faster (Figure 5A–C), causing a progressive increase in the N/C ratio from 8% to 9% in an hour (representing a 6% increase of the N/C ratio at 15 min and a 16% increase by 60 min)(Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The concentrations of large ribosomal subunits Rpl3001 and Rpl2401 increased progressively in the nucleus so that by 60 min of LMB treatment, nuclear and cytoplasmic levels were similar.
source: We found that the concentrations of large ribosomal subunits Rpl3001 and Rpl2401 tagged with the GFP (Knapp et al., 2019) increased progressively in the nucleus so that by 60 min of LMB treatment, nuclear and cytoplasmic levels were similar (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by fluorescence data in Figure 5F.

claim: A small ribosomal subunit protein Rps2-GFP showed little accumulation in the nucleus after LMB treatment.
source: In contrast, a small ribosomal subunit protein Rps2-GFP (Knapp et al., 2019), which was not expected to be affected by LMB (Aitchison and Rout, 2000), showed little accumulation in the nucleus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: The cytoplasmic intensities of ribosomal markers decreased slightly by 45 min of LMB treatment.
source: The cytoplasmic intensities of these three ribosomal markers decreased slightly by 45 min (Rpl3001 –19%, Rpl2401 –11% and Rps2-GFP –8%, Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-F; right panel), which may be due to redistribution into the nucleus, as well through ribosomal turnover or impaired biogenesis.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with interpretation.

claim: LMB-treated cells only exhibited a small (~8%) increase at 60 min in the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic protein staining compared to control cells.
source: LMB-treated cells only exhibited a small (~8%) increase at 60 min in the ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic protein staining compared to control cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from FITC staining data.

claim: Effective diffusion coefficient of nuclear GEMs showed a small but significant initial decrease at 15 min of LMB treatment, but it subsequently returned to a normal level at 60 min.
source: Deff of nuclear GEMs showed a small but significant initial decrease at 15 min of LMB treatment, but it subsequently returned to a normal level at 60 min (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from GEMs diffusion measurements.

claim: The cytoplasmic GEMs effective diffusion coefficient did not change significantly at 15 min of LMB treatment, but increased significantly at 30 and 60 min.
source: In contrast, the cytGEMs Deff did not change significantly at 15 min, but increased significantly at 30 and 60 min.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from GEMs diffusion measurements.

claim: LMB may lead to cytoplasmic dilution by inhibiting export of macromolecules such as mRNA out of the nucleus, leading to a decrease in protein synthesis, all while cells continue growing in volume at a normal rate.
source: LMB may lead to cytoplasmic dilution by inhibiting export of macromolecules such as mRNA out of the nucleus, leading to a decrease in protein synthesis, all while cells continue growing in volume at a normal rate (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F, Neurohr et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental observations, supported by citation.

claim: Protoplasts showed a similar increase in the N/C ratio in response to LMB as whole cells.
source: Protoplasts showed a similar increase in the N/C ratio in response to LMB (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from protoplast experiments.

claim: The elevated N/C ratio after LMB treatment was maintained upon osmotic shocks in protoplasts.
source: The elevated N/C ratio was maintained upon osmotic shocks (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–F); for instance, after 60 min of LMB treatment, protoplasts maintained an elevated N/C ratio of 10% over a range of hypoosmotic and hyperosmotic conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from osmotic shift experiments on LMB-treated protoplasts.

claim: In cells treated with LMB, the normalized non-osmotic volumes in the nucleus and cytoplasm were maintained at 25%.
source: BVH plots (Figure 5I) showed that in cells treated with LMB, the normalized non-osmotic volumes in the nucleus and cytoplasm were maintained at 25%.
evidence: This is a measurement from BVH plot analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: As nuclear volume increased after LMB treatment, the total amount of non-osmotic volume (dry mass) increased proportionally so that its ratio remained constant.
source: Thus, as nuclear volume increased, the total amount of non-osmotic volume (i.e. dry mass) increased proportionally so that its ratio remained constant.
evidence: This is an inference from the BVH plot data.

claim: The nuclei still behaved as ideal osmometers at the 15, 30, and 60 min timepoints after LMB treatment.
source: BVH plots also showed that the nuclei still behaved as ideal osmometers at the 15, 30, and 60 min timepoints (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G–J), indicating that membrane tension of the nucleus remained low throughout the time course.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from BVH plot analysis.

claim: At a low dosage of cycloheximide, interphase cells continued to grow in volume but at slower rates.
source: At this relatively low dosage, interphase cells continued to grow in volume but at slower rates (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from CHX treatment experiments.

claim: The nuclei also grew at the same slower rate as cells during CHX treatment, maintaining the N/C ratio.
source: The nuclei also grew at the same slower rate, maintaining the N/C ratio (Kume et al., 2017, Figure 6C, D and E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data and citation.

claim: GEMs analyses revealed that effective diffusion coefficient of nuclear and cytoplasmic GEMs increased proportionally during CHX treatment.
source: GEMs analyses revealed that Deff of nuclear and cytoplasmic GEMs increased proportionally (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from GEMs diffusion measurements.

claim: FITC staining showed no change in the ratio of nucleoplasmic to cytoplasmic distribution of total protein and RNA during CHX treatment.
source: Quantification of total protein and RNA on FITC stained cells showed no change in the ratio of nucleoplasmic to cytoplasmic distribution (ratio ~1) (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from FITC staining data.

claim: FITC staining without the RNA signal indicated a progressive decrease in concentration of total protein in both the nucleus and cytoplasm during CHX treatment, leading to a ~30% decrease in total protein concentration in both compartments after 1 hr.
source: However, FITC staining without the RNAs signal indicated a progressive decrease in concentration of total protein in both the nucleus and cytoplasm (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–G), leading to a ~30% decrease in total protein concentration in both compartments after 1 hr of CHX treatment.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from FITC staining data.

claim: The proportionate dilution of macromolecular components in both compartments did not alter the N/C ratio during CHX treatment.
source: These findings demonstrated that the proportionate dilution of macromolecular components in both compartments did not alter the N/C ratio.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the CHX treatment experiments.

claim: The N/C ratio is maintained with little variability, with a coefficient of variation of ~0.1.
source: The N/C ratio is maintained with little variability, with a coefficient of variation of ~0.1 (Figure 7A, WT).
evidence: This is a measurement from population data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The growth rate of fission yeast cells is largely exponential in character, such that large cells grow faster than smaller ones.
source: Like many other cell types, the growth rate of fission yeast cells is largely exponential in character, such that large cells grow faster than smaller ones (Knapp et al., 2019; Pickering et al., 2019; Tzur et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: S. pombe cells exhibit homeostasis behavior to maintain nuclear scaling.
source: Indeed, it was recently reported that S. pombe cells exhibit homeostasis behavior to maintain nuclear scaling (Cantwell and Nurse, 2019a; Neumann and Nurse, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: pom1∆ mutant cells display variable N/C ratios because of asymmetric cell division.
source: We measured homeostasis behavior in pom1∆ mutant cells, which display variable N/C ratios because of asymmetric cell division (Bähler and Pringle, 1998; Cantwell and Nurse, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is the basis for using this mutant.

claim: pom1∆ cells exhibited normal mitosis that produced two equally sized nuclei, but often placed their division septum asymmetrically, yielding daughters that were born with either too low or too high N/C ratios.
source: Time lapse images showed that these cells exhibited normal mitosis that produced two equally sized nuclei, but often placed their division septum asymmetrically, yielding daughters that were born with either too low or too high N/C ratios (Figure 7A–B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: An asynchronous population of pom1∆ cells displayed the same average N/C ratio as wildtype but with a ~threefold larger standard deviation.
source: Consistent with this, an asynchronous population of pom1∆ cells displayed the same average N/C ratio as wildtype but with a ~threefold larger standard deviation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a measurement from population data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cells born with abnormally large N/C ratios (>10) or abnormally small ratios (<7) gradually corrected their N/C ratio over time.
source: Cells born with abnormally large N/C ratios (>10) or abnormally small ratios (<7) gradually corrected their N/C ratio over time (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), consistent with previous findings (Cantwell and Nurse, 2019a).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from time-lapse tracking, consistent with literature.

claim: Cell growth rate was independent of their N/C ratio.
source: Cell growth rate was independent of their N/C ratio (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Nuclear growth rate was dependent on the N/C ratio: in cells with high N/C ratios nuclei grew slower than those in cells with normal N/C ratios, while nuclei in cells with low N/C ratios grew faster.
source: In contrast, nuclear growth rate was dependent on the N/C ratio: in cells with high N/C ratios nuclei grew slower than those in cells with normal N/C ratios, while nuclei in cells with low N/C ratios grew faster (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The continued growth of the cell and nucleus is sufficient to explain the observed correction of the N/C ratio without having to invoke an active mechanism.
source: These findings show that the continued growth of the cell and nucleus is sufficient to explain the observed correction of the N/C ratio without having to invoke an active mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the homeostasis experiments and modeling.

claim: The correction rates are on the time scales of growth rates, and thus large perturbations in N/C ratio were only partially corrected during a single cell cycle period.
source: The correction rates are on the time scales of growth rates, and thus large perturbations in N/C ratio were only partially corrected during a single cell cycle period.
evidence: This is an observation from the homeostasis experiments.

claim: This osmotic-based model has zero free parameters.
source: This model, which has zero free parameters, postulates that nuclear size is dictated in part by the numbers of osmotically active molecules in the nucleus and cytoplasm that cannot readily diffuse through the nuclear membranes (Figure 1; see Appendix).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's properties.

claim: In fission yeast, the nucleus readily changes in volume under osmotic perturbations, thus behaving as a near-ideal osmometer, indicating that contributions of membrane tension of the nuclear envelope on nuclear size are negligible (or very small).
source: In fission yeast, we determined that the nucleus readily changes in volume under osmotic perturbations, thus behaving as a near-ideal osmometer (Figure 2E); this behavior indicates that contributions of membrane tension of the nuclear envelope on nuclear size are negligible (or very small).
evidence: This is a conclusion from experimental observations.

claim: In fission yeast, the number of nuclear solutes is predicted to be about 8% of the total in the cell, giving rise to an average N/C ratio of 8%.
source: in the case of fission yeast, the number of these nuclear solutes is predicted to be about 8% of the total in the cell, giving rise to an average N/C ratio of 8%.
evidence: This is a prediction/conclusion from the model applied to fission yeast.

claim: The N/C ratio arises because the cell globally maintains the relative quantities of nuclear to cytoplasmic solutes by protein expression and transport.
source: The N/C ratio arises because the cell globally maintains the relative quantities of nuclear to cytoplasmic solutes by protein expression and transport.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model.

claim: During cell growth, the nucleus grows at the same rate as the cell because its growth is driven by the synthesis and transport of the nuclear macromolecules that contribute to osmotic pressure.
source: During cell growth, the nucleus grows at the same rate as the cell because its growth is driven by the synthesis and transport of the nuclear macromolecules that contribute to osmotic pressure.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model.

claim: The gradual correction of the N/C ratio by growth is reminiscent of 'adder behavior' for cell size homeostasis.
source: The gradual correction of the N/C ratio by growth is reminiscent of 'adder behavior' for cell size homeostasis (Campos et al., 2014; Taheri-Araghi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to another biological phenomenon, supported by citations.

claim: The primary function of nuclear size control is perhaps not to specify a certain size, but to maintain healthy levels of macromolecular crowding in the nucleoplasm.
source: This proposed view suggests that the primary function of nuclear size control is perhaps not to specify a certain size, but to maintain healthy levels of macromolecular crowding in the nucleoplasm (Ellis, 2001).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: The nuclear and cytoplasmic environments have similar degrees of mesoscale macromolecular crowding and similar concentrations of non-osmotic volumes.
source: Our osmotic perturbations and GEMs measurements showed that the nuclear and cytoplasmic environments, which contain quite different components, nevertheless have similar degrees of mesoscale macromolecular crowding and similar concentrations of non-osmotic volumes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from experimental measurements.

claim: Even after long exposure to LMB, when cells exhibit a significative higher N/C ratio, the normalized non-osmotic volumes of the nucleus and crowding in the nucleoplasm are similar to those in control cells.
source: Even after long exposure to LMB, when cells exhibit a significative higher N/C ratio (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), the normalized non-osmotic volumes of the nucleus and crowding in the nucleoplasm are similar to those in control cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from LMB treatment experiments.

claim: The osmotic nature of nuclear size control allows nucleoplasm and cytoplasm to stay in balance through not only synthesis and transport but also by osmotic control of nuclear volume.
source: The osmotic nature of nuclear size control thus allows nucleoplasm and cytoplasm to stay in balance through not only synthesis and transport but also by osmotic control of nuclear volume.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the findings.

claim: Osmotic-based models for nuclear size control have been proposed previously.
source: Osmotic-based models for nuclear size control have been proposed (Churney, 1942; Kim et al., 2016), including a recent theoretical report (Deviri and Safran, 2022) that evaluates the potential colloid osmotic force contributions of chromatin (1.5 Pa), chromatin counterions (20 Pa), and proteins (8 kPa) to support a similar osmotic model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: This study provides quantitative experimental validation of osmotic models in a cell type in which nuclear size happens to be primarily dictated by colloid osmotic forces.
source: Our studies here provide quantitative experimental validation in a cell type in which nuclear size happens to be primarily dictated by colloid osmotic forces.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the study.

claim: Under crowded conditions, colloid osmotic pressures generated by contact-interactions between macromolecules may predominate those generated by counterions.
source: However, under crowded conditions, colloid osmotic pressures generated by contact-interactions between macromolecules may predominate those generated by counterions (Mitchison, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: This osmotic-based mechanism is likely the primary factor in nuclear scaling mechanisms in mammalian and other cell types.
source: This osmotic-based mechanism is likely the primary factor in nuclear scaling mechanisms in mammalian and other cell types.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other systems.

claim: Osmotic shift experiments in mammalian chondrocytes cells reveal that the nucleus in these cells is not an ideal osmometer, but is restricted from swelling due to hypoosmotic shocks because of nuclear membrane tension.
source: Osmotic shift experiments in mammalian chondrocytes cells (Finan et al., 2009) reveal that the nucleus in these cells is not an ideal osmometer, but is restricted from swelling due to hypoosmotic shocks because of nuclear membrane tension.
evidence: This claim is based on reinterpretation of data from a cited study.

claim: The BVH plot from a mammalian chondrocytes study can be fitted with the model assuming a substantial nuclear membrane tension of σN = 0.02 N/m.
source: Indeed, the BVH plot in this paper (Figure 1A of Finan et al., 2009) can be fitted with our model assuming NN=4.10–16 mol and a substantial nuclear membrane tension of σN = 0.02 N/m.
evidence: This is a reanalysis of published data using the current model.

claim: Additional nuclear membrane tension in mammalian cells may be due to nuclear lamina, peri-nuclear actin and/or perinuclear chromatin forces acting on the nuclear envelope, which may be absent or reduced in fission yeast.
source: This additional nuclear membrane tension may be due to nuclear lamina, peri-nuclear actin and/or perinuclear chromatin forces acting on the nuclear envelope (Edens et al., 2017; Newport et al., 1990; Schreiner et al., 2015), which may be absent or reduced in fission yeast .
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between cell types, supported by citations.

claim: It is likely that osmotic forces act in concert with other mechanical elements to set nuclear size in more complex systems.
source: Thus, it is likely that osmotic forces act in concert with other mechanical elements to set nuclear size in these more complex systems.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the generality of the mechanism.

claim: Models similar to the one presented can even account for bacterial nucleoid size scaling.
source: We note that models similar to ours can even account for bacterial nucleoid size scaling (Gray et al., 2019), where instead of a nuclear envelope tension term, a partition coefficient establishes the equilibrium concentration of molecules between the cytoplasm and the nucleoid/nucleus.
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of similar models to other systems, supported by citation.
